en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Sappāṇakavagga 64.
The Training Rule on What is Gross.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta, having committed an intentional offense of emitting semen, informed a bhikkhu who was his brother’s student:
“Friend, I have committed an intentional offense of emitting semen.
Do not tell anyone.”
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu, having committed an offense of intentional emission of semen, requested a period of probation from the Saṅgha for that offense.
The Saṅgha granted him probation for that offense.
While he was undergoing probation, he saw that bhikkhu and said this to him:
“Friends, having committed an intentional offense of emitting semen, I requested the Saṅgha for probation for that offense;
the Saṅgha granted me probation for that offense. I am currently undergoing probation.
Friends, I acknowledge it; may the Venerable One remember me as one who acknowledges it.”
“Friend, does anyone else who commits this same offense act in this way?
“Yes, friend.
“Friend, this venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta, having committed an intentional emission of semen, informs me [of it], saying, ‘Do not inform anyone.’”
“But why, friend, did you conceal it?
“It is so, friends.
Then that bhikkhu informed the bhikkhus of this matter.
Those monks who were modest … [as above] … complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How can a monk knowingly conceal a grave offense of another monk?
… [as above] … “Is it true, monk, that you knowingly concealed a grave offense of a monk?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, knowingly conceal a grave offense of a bhikkhu? This is not suitable…” [and so on].
“Monk, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence… [as before]… And thus,
monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘If any monk, knowing it to be a grave offense, should conceal another monk’s offense, he commits an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).’”
"But whoever" means whoever such as this...
"a monk."
...pe... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"Of a bhikkhu" means of another bhikkhu.
"Knows" means he knows it himself, or others inform him of it, or he informs [others] himself.
"Gross offense" (duṭṭhulla-āpatti) means...
The four *pārājika* offenses and the thirteen *saṅghādisesa* offenses.
"Should conceal" means:

thinking, "Knowing this, they will accuse me, reprove me, revile me, mock me, or make me feel dejected; I will not tell," at the mere moment of relinquishing the burden [of confession], there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If one conceals a grave offense while perceiving it as a grave offense, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one conceals a grave offense while being uncertain of it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one conceals a grave offense while perceiving it as a non-grave offense, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one conceals a non-gross offense, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one conceals an impropriety—whether gross or non-gross—of one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If, regarding a non-gross offense, one perceives it as a gross offense, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is a non-grave offense and he is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is a non-grave offense and he perceives it as a non-grave offense, there is an offense of wrong-doing. There is no offense—
If one does not report, thinking, "There will be strife, quarreling, contention, or dispute in the Saṅgha";
or if one does not report, thinking, "There will be a schism in the Saṅgha or a fracture in the Saṅgha";
or if one does not report, thinking, "This person is harsh and cruel, and will cause an obstacle to life or an obstacle to the holy life."
He does not report because he sees no other suitable monks;
he does not report because he does not wish to conceal it;
he does not report thinking, "He will be known by his own deed."
"In the case of one who is insane,
or in the case of the first offender.
The fourth training rule on grave offenses is finished.
